messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Richard's Case

Richard Castellano was sixty-five years old and had spent thirty-eight years in the District Attorney's office, building a reputation as a meticulous prosecutor who believed deeply in the rule of law. That belief had been shattered one evening in March, four months before he came to see me, when two uniformed officers stopped him as he left a restaurant in downtown Philadelphia. He had been meeting a colleague to discuss a case—nothing unusual, nothing wrong. But one officer had mistaken him for a suspect in an armed robbery three blocks away. When Richard, accustomed to authority and confident in his standing, had questioned the stop and asked to see the warrant, the situation escalated with a speed that still left him breathless to recount. The officer had shoved him against the brick wall of the restaurant, hard enough that his shoulder struck the corner of a window frame. His glasses fell. For thirty seconds—though it felt longer—Richard was pinned there while the second officer ran his information. When they realized their error, they apologized curtly and left. Richard stood on the sidewalk, bleeding slightly from his shoulder, his hands shaking. He had been violated by the very institution he had spent his career serving.

In the weeks that followed, Richard's world contracted. He became consumed by a vigilant scanning of his surroundings, a constant monitoring of the people around him. At the grocery store, he watched other shoppers with an intensity that bordered on obsessive, reading their faces and postures for signs of aggression or threat. On the street, his eyes tracked police cars the moment he heard a siren. He had come to believe that the world was fundamentally unsafe, that authority could turn on him without warning, and that ordinary people harbored dangerous impulses he needed to detect before they acted. When he encountered someone behaving rudely—a cashier speaking sharply, a driver cutting him off—the violation of basic civility triggered a cascade of fear. These small moral infractions felt like proof of the chaos beneath society's surface, and his mind raced to interpret them as precursors to violence. Each instance of perceived misbehavior seemed to confirm his new certainty: people were capable of harm, and he was vulnerable to it.

The hypervigilance and threat-focused watching intensified his anxiety to unbearable levels. To manage the mounting dread, Richard began using sensory distraction as a buffer. He would turn on loud music or the television the moment he came home, drowning out the silence that allowed his mind to spiral. He also found himself repeatedly seeking reassurance from his wife, Margaret—asking her over and over whether she thought he was okay, whether she believed he was safe, whether what had happened to him meant he was in real danger. Margaret, exhausted and confused, would reassure him, but the relief lasted only minutes before the doubt crept back in. Yet these very coping strategies—the loud noise, the reassurance-seeking—paradoxically kept him trapped. The constant stimulation prevented him from habituating to the fear; the reassurance-seeking reinforced his underlying belief that he needed external validation to feel safe. And because he was using these tools to manage his threat perception, he never truly confronted or questioned the catastrophic interpretations driving it. Instead, the cycle tightened. He would lower his guard slightly, only to hear an incomprehensible fragment of conversation—overlapping voices in a coffee shop, a police radio crackling outside—and the sensory confusion would trigger a fresh wave of threat-monitoring. He would scan the room more intently, watching faces, listening for tone, searching for the danger he was now certain was lurking.

His work had begun to suffer. Richard found himself unable to concentrate during depositions, his attention fragmenting whenever someone raised their voice or when unexpected noise erupted in the hallway. He had taken a leave of absence two months ago, telling his supervisor he had a shoulder injury that needed rest. Margaret knew the truth. She watched her husband of forty years become someone she barely recognized—wired, suspicious, dependent on her reassurance, unable to sleep through the night. Richard himself felt the weight of the transformation. He had always been rational, controlled, certain of his place in the world. Now he was afraid of the very fabric of ordinary life. It was this realization—that he had become a prisoner of his own vigilance—that finally brought him to my office, hoping that someone could help him understand why a single moment of violation had unmade him so completely, and whether he could ever feel safe again.
